Interior cameras must be positioned to show key architectural features like windows and daylight sources.

Furniture in a living room must be selected from a cohesive set or style family; if a piece clashes with the main sofa and other seating, it must be swapped for a model that matches the room's established style.
Furniture in a bedroom or living space must be selected from a cohesive set or style family; if a piece clashes with the room's color palette and style, it must be swapped for a model that matches.
Furniture models must be high-quality, finished assets; low-poly placeholder boxes with grid textures are not acceptable for client presentation.
Kitchen counters must be connected to walls or islands to form a coherent set; isolated bare slabs are not acceptable.

Exterior renders must use high-quality landscaping models (trees, ground) and accurate architectural details; crude 'lollipop' trees and flat untextured ground are not acceptable for client presentation.
Exterior views from interior windows must show a high-quality landscape, not crude low-poly 'lollipop' trees.
A kitchen render must show its anchor appliances (cooktop, fridge, wall cabinets) and the exterior visible through its windows must use the project's site model, not a placeholder landscape.
An interior camera must be placed inside its room, aimed at the room's main furniture group, with a lens that frames the whole group, not a blank wall.

A bathroom render must show its fixtures and accessories, and the exterior visible through its windows must use the project's site model, not a placeholder landscape.
Furniture in a room must be from a coherent collection (matching style and scale); the exterior visible through its windows must use the project's site model.
A hall/entrance must contain its functional pieces (shoe cabinet, etc.) and decor; the exterior visible through its windows must use the project's site model.

Every interior camera must be placed inside its room's clear volume (at least 0.5 m from any wall or piece) and aimed at the room's centre, so the render shows the room's function, not a wall or a door face.
A decor item that penetrates its host by more than 0.03 m must be re-seated (or removed) in the next furniture round rather than left unbuilt.
A sideboard or console must be centred on its wall span (or paired with a companion piece) so the composition is balanced, not pushed into a corner with a bare wall beside it.
A single armchair must be placed as part of a seating group (facing the coffee table or sofa), not flat against a wall under a window.
A washbasin must be anchored to a counter or wall (its base resting on a surface), never floating; if the model reads as a floating slab, re-seat it in the next round.
The exterior ground must carry a real ground material (grass, soil, paving) rather than a flat untextured plane.
The DWG reader must read ATTDEF (attribute definition) entities and map them to the block/label they define, so attribute text is not silently dropped from the ledger.
Site decor read on an upper level must be placed on that level's site (or explicitly suppressed with a reason), not silently dropped because the site is modelled at the ground floor.
When a room outline holds two labels, the reading must split it into two rooms at the label boundary rather than keeping one label as a second name of the other room.
Every printed area label in the documents must be matched to its room and used in the area check, so a printed area is never silently lost.
When walls are drawn as face lines, the reader must also consider wall primitives on runner-up layers (e.g. DUVAR) and off-layer primitives, not only the chosen layer, so no wall segment is left out.

Armchairs should be part of a seating arrangement, not pushed flat against a wall under a window; they should be angled towards the center of the room or the coffee table.
Kitchen fittings (sink, wall cabinets) should be built at the library level (with proper textures and details) rather than falling back to parametric meshes when no library model is available.
Toilet models in the library should include seat covers and basic decor (e.g., spare toilet paper) to avoid a sterile, incomplete appearance in renders.
Bathroom fixtures and tiles should be selected from a higher-quality library set to avoid a cheap, institutional look in renders.
Bed models in the library should include more substantial headboards and frames to avoid a plain, low-profile appearance in client-ready renders.
Nightstand models in the library should be more stylish and cohesive with the room's furniture set to avoid a generic, unstyled appearance.
Door models in the library should include more detailed handles and finishes to avoid a cheap, generic appearance in stylish projects.

A stair or landing that is the only vertical circulation of a level must be built with a full parametric stair model (treads, risers, stringers and a proper balustrade), never as a bare platform with a glass guard; a platform-only representation is a defect, not a style choice.

Interior doors must be built with a styled door model (panelled or flush with a proper frame and handle) matching the project's finish, never as a plain flat slab; a generic slab door is a defect in a client presentation.
A floor lamp must be built with a proper library model (a real lamp with a shade and stem), never as a low-poly box placeholder; a placeholder lamp is a defect.

Exterior wall surfaces and plinths must be built with textured materials (stone, render, brick) matching the project's finish, never as untextured flat surfaces; bare material is a defect in a client presentation.
A stone path or paving leading to an entrance must be built with a textured paving model, never as a rough untextured mesh with visible cracks; a placeholder path is a defect.

A sofa placed under a sloped ceiling must be fitted to the ceiling clearance at its position (max height = ceiling - 0.05 m); the fit check must reject any model whose height exceeds that clearance before the swap is accepted, and the catalogue must offer at least one sofa variant per room whose height fits the minimum ceiling clearance of the room's sloped zone.

Site trees must use high-poly, photorealistic models from the library (not low-poly lollipop placeholders); the site stage must select tree models that match the project's render quality standard, and the catalogue must include at least one photorealistic tree variant per tree type used in the project.
The exterior landscape must use a realistic terrain and tree model (not low-poly placeholder blobs) so that views through doors and windows read as a real site, not a placeholder.

The site stage must reject low-poly placeholder vegetation (lollipop/blob trees) and only place library models that match the project's photorealistic render standard; a placeholder asset must never be built into the scene.
The furniture agent must select coffee table models that match the room's color palette (pale/muted tones) and avoid clashing wood tones like bright honey-oak when the floor is pale.
The site stage must reject low-poly placeholder vegetation and only place library models that match the project's photorealistic render standard.

Bed groups in bedrooms should be symmetric (nightstand on both sides) unless spatial constraints explicitly prevent it; the layout solver must verify this symmetry during placement.
Paired furniture items (like armchairs) must use the same model or a visually coherent set to ensure stylistic consistency.

Floor lamps must be selected with a scale appropriate to the room's ceiling height and must not obstruct window views or door swings; models with oversized shades or incorrect proportions are prohibited.
Exterior environments visible through windows must use realistic, high-fidelity assets; low-poly or placeholder trees and ground planes are prohibited in final renders.

Entrance halls must be furnished with appropriate items (shoe cabinet, console, lighting) to avoid looking like bare shells; the furniture agent must verify that all halls have a minimum set of decorative and functional pieces.
Staircases and railings must be selected from a catalogue of styled models that match the project's design language; generic or default placeholder models are prohibited.
Interior cameras must be positioned to show the room's layout and key furniture, avoiding close-up corner shots that cut off main pieces.
All doors must be modeled with frames and hardware (handles, hinges) to appear finished; flat slab doors without details are prohibited.
Furniture within a room must be stylistically coherent; the furniture agent must ensure that major pieces (sofa, bench, etc.) share a common style or material palette.
Lighting fixtures must match the room's style; the furniture agent must select lamps that are stylistically consistent with the other furniture in the room.
Interior cameras must be positioned to show key architectural features like windows and daylight sources.

Ground surfaces must have texture and detail to avoid a 'video game' aesthetic; flat untextured planes are prohibited in final renders.

Furniture in a bedroom or living space must be selected from a cohesive set or style family; if a piece clashes with the room's color palette and style, it must be swapped for a model that matches.

Kitchen counters must be connected to walls or islands to form a coherent set; isolated bare slabs are not acceptable.

Exterior views from interior windows must show a high-quality landscape, not crude low-poly 'lollipop' trees.

rules_proposed.rule: Scene checks must pass; if a check fails, the build stage must be re-run to fix the geometry.
The exterior ground must be textured and realistic, not a flat, untextured plane.
null
A wet-room fixture that reads as floating or cut off at a wall edge must be re-placed against its host wall or counter in the next agent round when its model is pinned and cannot be swapped.
A decorative accent that clashes with the room's stated palette and whose model is pinned must be replaced in the next agent round with a model that passes the room's height and fit caps.
The exterior ground plane must carry a textured material (grass, soil, or paver) rather than a flat untextured colour, so it does not read as a default viewport floor.

When two openings on the same wall are separated by less than 1.20 m, the layout engine must verify that the intervening wall span can accommodate a 0.60 m clear walkway; if not, it must propose moving one of the openings or adjusting the room layout to create the required clearance.

When a bed's headboard is not flush against a wall (offset > 0.02 m), the layout engine must snap it to the nearest wall if the move is within 0.30 m, or flag it for manual review if the move exceeds the drawn-lock tolerance.

When a piece blocks a door swing, the layout engine must move the piece to the nearest free position that does not intersect the door's swing arc, prioritizing positions along the wall opposite the door.

When a piece blocks a window, the layout engine must move the piece to the nearest free position that does not obstruct the window's view or access, prioritizing positions along the wall opposite the window.

When a door and a window on the same wall are separated by less than 1.20 m, the layout engine must verify that the intervening wall span can accommodate a 0.60 m clear walkway; if not, it must propose moving one of the openings or adjusting the room layout to create the required clearance.
When a desk is rendered as a floating slab, the render engine must verify that the model includes legs or support structure; if not, it must swap to a model that includes them.
A piece's free zone in front of it must not be blocked by another piece; the furniture agent must re-place the blocking piece or the piece itself to restore the clearance.
The main walkway from the entrance door must be at least 0.80 m wide; the furniture agent must re-place pieces to widen the path.
A dresser's back must be on a wall; the furniture agent must re-place it to snap to the wall.
A nightstand must not overlap a bed; the furniture agent must re-place it to clear the collision.
A bed must have at least 0.60 m of clearance on its sides; the furniture agent must re-place it to restore the clearance.
A wardrobe's front use zone must be reachable by a 0.60 m walkway; the furniture agent must re-place it to restore access.
A shower must not stand in front of a window; the furniture agent must re-place it to clear the opening.
A sofa's free zone in front of it must not be blocked by another piece; the furniture agent must re-place the blocking piece or the sofa itself to restore the clearance.
A floor lamp must not stand in front of a window; the furniture agent must re-place it to clear the opening.
A bathtub's back must be on a wall; the furniture agent must re-place it to snap to the wall.
A washbasin's back must be on a wall; the furniture agent must re-place it to snap to the wall.
A washing machine's front use zone must be reachable by a 0.60 m walkway; the furniture agent must re-place it to restore access.
The exterior environment must be believable for a client presentation; the site must include textured ground, a realistic sky, and high-poly trees.
An opening must have a proper frame; the correct_geometry tool can fix the opening frame.

A decor item that penetrates its host by more than 0.03 m must be re-seated (or removed) in the next furniture round rather than left unbuilt.
A washbasin must be anchored to a counter or wall (its base resting on a surface), never floating; if the model reads as a floating slab, re-seat it in the next round.
